problem: Reactive and LSTM-based DRL policies for goal-image visual navigation cannot hold long-term memory of the environment layout, so they learn slowly and fail when the goal is hundreds of steps away. Metric maps are hard to learn, and prior topological-map work relies on explicit Dijkstra planning plus supervised waypoint following.
motivation: Accurate metric measurements are often unnecessary for navigation, and a topological graph built from aimless exploration is a cheap, agent-agnostic environment prior. If the graph can be turned into a learned feature that signals where the goal lies relative to the agent, it can give reward-sparse RL a long-range guiding signal.
key_idea: Build a topological graph memory from exploration images with a learned connectivity classifier, then use recurrent graph attention over it to produce a guided feature (current-node minus goal-node aggregated features) that feeds an A2C policy trained end-to-end.
insight: In the harder maze 2, where the goal is far away, all baselines (FF-nogoal, FF-goal, LSTM-nogoal) reach only 10% success, while GAM reaches 100%. This suggests the graph-propagated goal signal helps most when random reward discovery fails. Reward curves also show faster learning. There is no ablation of the graph, attention or the number of iterations K, so the causal attribution is only indirect.
method: Memory construction: a ResNet-18 siamese encoder plus 5 FC layers is trained as a binary connectivity classifier. Positive pairs are frames with 5<=k-t<=20 in the exploration trajectory. Nodes are the embeddings of exploration frames, and edges connect the top-L most probable pairs (L=1300 for maze1, 1800 for maze2).

Localization: the current observation and the goal image are matched to graph nodes by classifier similarity. The median node among the top-L similar nodes is chosen to reduce jitter, with no GT position used.

Graph attention: a siamese attention network psi(x_i,x_j) gives softmax coefficients over neighbors (including self). Node features are aggregated as x_i' = sum alpha_ij x_j, and several attention heads are concatenated.

Recurrent aggregation: the aggregation is iterated K times with shared weights, so goal features flow to the current node. The paper proves convergence via a random walk / Markov chain argument (irreducible and aperiodic stochastic matrix).
Guided attention feature: eta_t = x_t^(K) - x_g^(K), concatenated with the observation features at the first FC layer of the policy.

DRL control: A2C with a 3-conv encoder, and attention weights trained jointly by the RL loss. Reward is +10 at goal and -0.05 per step. There are 7 discrete actions and the agent is re-spawned upon reaching the goal.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 + FC connectivity classifier (supervised); small conv encoder + graph attention + A2C actor-critic (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Exploration images from manually controlled aimless exploration of ViZDoom mazes (400 wall-texture variants per layout) for graph construction; RL trained for 5e7 steps
setting.observation: 84x84 gray-scale first-person RGB image plus goal image
setting.action_space: 7 discrete low-level actions (move forward/backward/left/right, turn left/right, no-op)
setting.privileged: none at test time (localization uses images only), but exploration images of the test maze are required as a prior

numbers.extra: 2000 test steps; success checked from all initial positions within 500 steps; uses exploration prior
6000 test steps; 10 initial positions; success checked within 500 steps; uses exploration prior

numbers_note: Only two custom ViZDoom mazes; baselines are not listed here. Learning curves are given in figures only.
results: GAM matches the baselines on maze 1 (SR 100%, score 132.05 vs 126.05 for LSTM-nogoal). On the harder maze 2 it reaches 100% SR (score 100.5), against 10% for all baselines (FF-nogoal, FF-goal, LSTM-nogoal). It also learns faster and generalizes to new start and goal positions, shown qualitatively.
limitations: Evaluated only on two small synthetic ViZDoom mazes against weak baselines (no comparison with metric-map or topological-graph methods such as SPTM), and no ablations
The graph is static and needs a prior exploration of the same environment. The paper also has no real-robot validation
The convergence theorem shows features converge to a stationary state, which is in tension with using finite K to keep node features distinguishable
